title: When Generated Information Returns: Error Persistence in LLM-Mediated Information Ecosystems
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 24 Oct 2026]
Title:When Generated Information Returns: Error Persistence in LLM-Mediated Information Ecosystems
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Large language models (LLMs) increasingly produce online articles from material that later becomes input to other models. This circulation connects individual responses to the information available for subsequent generation. We study a consequential distinction: an article can avoid endorsing a false claim while preserving the concrete details that enable its reproduction. Our framework connects claim content, expressed stance, and downstream reuse to explain selective error persistence under a continuing supply of accurate and inaccurate information. We implement a controlled community writing process that varies whether published articles return as inputs, matching external supply, input capacity, and generation volume. Across twelve factual targets and four production models, recirculation increases the presence of complete false claims by 7.29 percentage points at the final round while reducing explicit endorsement by 8.33 points. Effects differ across facts and models. Paired interventions then abstract eligible error details within fixed histories while preserving correct content and the surrounding controversy. Error reproduction remains largely unchanged across the evaluation targets, while a development quotation target exhibits local reductions. These findings connect persistent errors to the information available throughout a writing process and motivate evaluation of both what models affirm and what their publications supply to future writers.

report.summary: A controlled study finds that when LLM-written articles are recirculated as future model inputs, complete false claims become more common even as explicit endorsement declines.
report.background: Generative AI is making article production cheap, and model-generated text increasingly enters the same web and publishing ecosystems that feed later models. This creates feedback loops: outputs become inputs, and errors can persist even without any single model strongly asserting them. Prior work on model collapse and synthetic-data contamination warns that recursive training can degrade information quality, but this paper examines a subtler pathway: articles may avoid endorsing a false claim while preserving concrete details that let later writers reproduce it. The study uses a controlled community writing process to test how recirculation, external information supply, input capacity, and generation volume interact. It matters for publishers, model developers, and platforms that rely on web-scale data, retrieval-augmented generation, and synthetic content, because error persistence may depend on the information supply chain rather than only on individual model outputs.
key_points: Recirculation increased complete false claims. Across 12 factual targets and four production models, returning published articles as inputs raised the presence of complete false claims by 7.29 percentage points at the final round, supporting concerns about self-reinforcing information loops.

Explicit endorsement declined. The same setup reduced explicit endorsement by 8.33 percentage points. This means an article can sound cautious or avoid asserting a falsehood while still carrying details that allow later writers or models to reproduce the error.

The design isolates recirculation. A controlled community writing process varied whether published articles returned as inputs while matching external supply, input capacity, and generation volume. Effects differed across facts and models, indicating selective rather than uniform error persistence.

Removing error details did not reliably stop reproduction. Paired interventions abstracted eligible error details within fixed histories while preserving correct content and surrounding controversy. Error reproduction remained largely unchanged across evaluation targets, with local reductions only in a development quotation target.

Evaluation should track what publications supply. The findings motivate assessing both what models affirm and what their outputs make available to future writers. Final-answer accuracy or stated stance alone may miss downstream contamination risks in LLM-mediated information ecosystems.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this shifts attention from single-output truthfulness to the integrity of the information ecosystem. Synthetic content, web corpora, and retrieval systems can recycle false details even when models avoid explicit endorsement. Developers should evaluate downstream reuse, separate stance from detail preservation, add provenance and recirculation controls, and test how outputs affect later generation. Publishers and platforms may need stronger source verification and content-lineage practices. For regular users, the practical warning is that a cautious tone does not guarantee accuracy: repeated false claims can circulate without being loudly asserted. Users should verify specific facts and sources rather than treating an absence of endorsement as evidence of reliability.
report.tools: To follow up, read the arXiv paper and use Connected Papers or Litmaps to trace related work on model collapse, synthetic-data contamination, and misinformation. For hands-on evaluation, try open-source Ragas, DeepEval, or promptfoo to build recirculation and stance-versus-detail tests. FEVER and AVeriTeC offer fact-checking datasets, while C2PA Content Credentials and invisible-watermark tools support provenance experiments. Also watch data-lineage and RAG observability tools.
